paragraphs.text: A green tea made in Japan in 1930, ninety-six years ago. The record names the country but not the prefecture where the leaf was grown.

Green tea is meant to be drunk within about a year of picking, or kept sealed for a year or two. No tradition of [ageing green tea](green:ageing) is recorded, and it does not mature the way pu’er or white tea can. A green tea this old was not made to last this long, so its keeping shaped it more than its making did, and how it was kept is not on record.
As a [green tea](green:definition), the leaf was heated soon after picking so that it never oxidised. In Japan that heat has usually come from [steam](green:styles) rather than a pan.

brewing.text: Green tea takes water well below the boil, about 80°C, a little cooler for the youngest leaf and a little warmer for older, larger leaf. Boiling water draws out bitterness and dries the cup. A common start is about 2 grams of leaf to 100 ml, in a glass or a small gaiwan, with short steeps of half a minute to two minutes, and the same leaf can be brewed a few times.

notice.text: A fresh, clean cup that many call crisp, with a sweet, soft finish, and a pale green to yellow-green liquor. The smell runs from fresh leaf to flowers, and steamed teas lean grassy or seaweed-like. Too much heat or too long a steep turns the cup bitter and drying.
